vignette:
Nadia Haddad is a 59-year-old police officer who came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to handle this on her own. She has spent most of her adult life in law enforcement, and before the assault she thought of herself as disciplined, steady, and hard to rattle. The event she returns to in sessions happened while she was off duty but still in a setting shaped by her work. She had been driving with another person in the car when an argument escalated into violence. What remains sharpest for her is not a broad outline but a sequence of exact details: the enclosed feel of the vehicle, the sense of being trapped beside someone whose movements were suddenly unpredictable, the pounding in her chest, and the sounds that marked the assault. When she describes it, she does not speak in generalities. She can hear the voice, the sudden change in tone, the impact noises, and her own breathing. Remembering it brings back the same terror she felt at the time, as if the event is not simply something she knows happened but something she is made to undergo again.

In the weeks afterward, Nadia noticed that certain moments could seize her before she had time to think. If her heart began racing for any reason, even from climbing stairs or hurrying through a shift, her attention fixed immediately on it. She had come to believe that her body had stopped acting like an ally; the pounding in her chest felt like proof that she was no longer truly safe, even when she was standing in a familiar room at work. She would stop and listen inwardly, tracking every beat and every surge of adrenaline, and then monitoring her thoughts just as closely. What frightened her most was the possibility that these reactions meant she was losing control or "going crazy." She began scanning her own mind for signs that she was slipping, testing whether her thoughts felt normal, whether she was staying oriented, whether she was still herself.

Driving became especially difficult when another person was in the car. The combination was too close to the assault: confined space, another body beside her, the need to stay alert while unable to simply leave. Even routine drives with colleagues could make her shoulders tighten and her pulse jump. She would grip the wheel, track every movement from the passenger seat, and feel her mind narrowing to danger. Violence in any form also caught her sharply. Calls, footage, raised voices, a sudden shove between civilians-anything that carried the shape of aggression could pull her back into the sensory certainty of what happened. In those moments she did not just think about the assault; she heard parts of it in her head, vividly and against her will.

Nadia's response over time was to make her world smaller. Although she is married, she cut off contact more broadly, withdrawing from friends and extended family and declining invitations she once would have attended. She told herself there was no point leaning on other people because people could not be relied on when it mattered. That belief fit too easily with her anger about the assault itself. She speaks with bitter clarity about how deeply unfair it was and about the fact that, in her view, nothing meaningful has been done about it. That sense of unresolved injustice sits close to the surface whenever she talks about the aftermath.

At work, the changes have become harder to hide. As a police officer she already worked in an environment where vigilance is valued, but Nadia describes a different kind of watching now-less tactical than relentless. She studies faces, postures, hands, distances, entrances, always checking for dangerous people. In the station parking lot, during calls, even walking through public buildings, her attention is pulled toward who might turn volatile. Riding with someone else or being assigned to situations where violence is possible leaves her braced before anything has happened. Colleagues have noticed she is quieter and less willing to socialize, and at home her withdrawal has left her husband feeling shut out, though she says little beyond insisting she is tired.

By the time she sought help, Nadia was exhausted by living in a body she felt she could not trust and among people she felt she could not rely on. The immediate reason for treatment was not one dramatic breakdown but the accumulation of too many moments in which a racing heart, a violent scene, or simply driving with another person made her feel overtaken by terror. She wants relief, but even in asking for it she is guarded. She is most afraid that these reactions will continue to ambush her and that she will never again feel secure in her own body or at ease around other people. At the same time, she still hopes that speaking about what happened in full detail might finally lead to a life that feels larger than vigilance, isolation, and the conviction that she must face all of this alone.
